title: “a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body” — who was he?
summary: Mark 14:51–52 says that at the arrest “there followed him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body”, that the young men laid hold on him, and that he “left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked”. The verses do not say who he was.
text: KJV Mark 14:51: “there followed him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body”. KJV Mark 14:52: “he left the linen cloth, and fled from them naked”. KJV Mark 14:50: “they all forsook him, and fled”.
reasoning: The man is introduced as “a certain young man” and not named, and the verses give no reason why he was there or why the incident is told. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV from Matthew to John finds the words “young man” at Matthew 19:20 and 19:22 (the one who asked what good thing he should do), Mark 14:51 and Mark 16:5 (the figure at the sepulchre). The incident is not told in the other Gospels that were searched. Possible readings, named only as readings: a follower of the disciples’ company who is otherwise unknown; a person of the household of the supper; the writer of the account. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted. The word search is a word search of one packaged KJV text covering the four Gospels and does not examine the Greek. The record does not say that any reading is the right one and does not claim that no other passage of the Bible says more.

title: “let him that readeth understand” — who is the reader, and what is he to understand?
summary: Mark 13:14 puts, in the middle of the saying about “the abomination of desolation”, the words “(let him that readeth understand,)”. The verse does not say who the reader is or what he is to read.
text: KJV Mark 13:14: “(let him that readeth understand,)”. KJV Matthew 24:15: “(whoso readeth, let him understand:)”. KJV Daniel 9:27: “for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate”.
reasoning: The parenthesis is addressed to a reader and does not say whether it is Jesus speaking to a hearer who will later read, or a remark of the writer to the one who reads the Gospel. It also does not say whether the reader is to read the book named in Matthew 24:15, which is Daniel by the KJV, or the Gospel. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “readeth” finds Habakkuk 2:2, Matthew 24:15, Mark 13:14 and Revelation 1:3, and only Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14 are in the Gospels. Possible readings, named only as readings: a remark of the writer of the Gospel; a direction of Jesus that the book named be read; an instruction that the hearer discern the sign. The record does not decide between them.

title: “every one shall be salted with fire” — who is meant, and what is the salting?
summary: Mark 9:49 says “For every one shall be salted with fire”, and 9:50 goes on “Salt is good” and “Have salt in yourselves”. The verses do not say who “every one” is or what being salted with fire is.
text: KJV Mark 9:49: “For every one shall be salted with fire”. KJV Mark 9:50: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another”. KJV Leviticus 2:13: “with all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt”.
reasoning: The verse follows the sayings about the fire that is not quenched (9:43–48) and gives its reason with “for”, but does not say whether “every one” is everyone, or those who are cast into the fire of 9:48, or those who follow. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV for “salted” finds Ezekiel 16:4, Matthew 5:13 and Mark 9:49, in which the word is used of a newborn child, of the salt of the earth, and here. No other verse of the three says what being salted with fire is. Possible readings, named only as readings: that the fire of testing preserves the faithful; that the fire is the judgment of the sayings before it; that the verse uses the sacrificial salt of Leviticus 2:13 as an image. The record does not decide between them.
